title: Count the days until a warmer day
text:
A weather app shows, next to each day of a forecast, how long you have to wait for warmer weather.

Write `daily_temperatures(temps)` that returns, for each day, how many days pass until a warmer day.

Input and output:
- `temps`: a list of 1 to 100,000 daily temperatures, each an integer from 30 to 100.
- Returns a list of integers, one per day, in the same order as `temps`.

Rules:
- For day `i`, find the first later day `j` whose temperature is strictly higher than `temps[i]`. The answer for day `i` is `j - i`.
- A later day with the same temperature is not warmer.
- If no later day is warmer, the answer for that day is 0. The last day's answer is always 0.
answer:
### Approach
Scan the days from left to right and keep a stack of the days still waiting for a warmer day. From the bottom of the stack to the top, their temperatures never rise, because a warmer day would already have settled the cooler days before it. When a new day arrives, it settles every waiting day on top of the stack that is strictly cooler: pop each one and record the distance. Then push the new day, which now waits too. A day with the same temperature does not pop anything, since equal is not warmer. Days still on the stack at the end never see a warmer day and keep 0.

Because temperatures run only from 30 to 100, a right-to-left scan also works. Remember the next day on which each temperature appears, and for each day take the nearest of the warmer ones. That is at most 70 checks per day, so it stays linear.

### Complexity
Each day is pushed once and popped at most once: O(n) time and O(n) space for the stack.
hints: For each day you need the nearest bigger value to its right. That question has a one-pass answer.
Keep the days that are still waiting for a warmer day. Their temperatures never rise from the oldest waiting day to the newest one, so a new day can only settle the most recent ones.
Scan left to right with a stack of waiting day indices. While the current day is warmer than the day on top, pop that day and record the distance between them. Then push the current day.
Pop only on a strictly higher temperature. Popping on an equal one gives the wrong wait for days that repeat a temperature.

approaches.name: Scan forward from every day
approaches.idea: For each day, walk right until a warmer day turns up.
approaches.limit: A long flat or falling stretch makes every day walk to the end, about 5 billion steps at 100,000 days.

approaches.name: Remember where each temperature appears next
approaches.idea: Scan right to left, keeping the next day for each temperature from 30 to 100, and take the nearest of the warmer ones.
approaches.limit: Works only because `k`, the number of possible temperatures, is 71. With any range of values it falls apart.

approaches.name: Stack of days still waiting
approaches.idea: Keep indices of days without an answer yet. Each new day pops and settles every cooler day on top, then waits itself.

algorithm: Make `answer`, a list of n zeros, and an empty stack of day indices. An array with push and pop works as the stack in every language.

For each day `i` from 0 to `n - 1`, in order: while the stack is not empty and `temps[i]` is strictly greater than `temps[top]`, where `top` is the index on top of the stack, pop `top` and set `answer[top] = i - top`.
When the scan ends, every index left on the stack has no warmer later day, so its answer stays 0.

followups.q: Return the warmer temperature itself instead of the wait.
followups.a: Record `temps[i]` instead of `i - top` when you pop. Days left on the stack get a marker such as -1.

followups.q: Now the forecast wraps around, so the first day follows the last one.
followups.a: Scan the indices twice, using `i % n`, and push only during the first pass. It stays O(n).

followups.q: Can you do it without a stack?
followups.a: Scan right to left. For day `i`, start at `j = i + 1` and, while `temps[j]` is not warmer and `answer[j]` is not 0, jump ahead by `answer[j]`, since the days in between are no warmer.

pitfalls: Pushing temperatures instead of day indices, so the distance can no longer be worked out.
Popping on an equal temperature, which treats a repeat of the same temperature as warmer.
Scanning forward from every day, which times out on a long flat or falling stretch.
